newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Digital TV changes European media landscape.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Digital TV changes European media landscape.

text.p: The brave new world of digital television is gradually invading Western Europe, hop-scotching across the continent as broadcasters find new markets for multi-channel offerings.
Already a reality on a small scale in France, Germany, Italy and Spain, digital TV is set to make a much bigger splash.
"In the future, all television will be digital," Robert Montgomery, managing director of Kagan World Media, a London-based research group, told Reuters. "This is just the advent."

What digital television means for viewers is more choices -- typically lots of movies and sporting events. For advertisers it means an increasingly fragmented market, demanding more choices in how they allocate advertising budgets.

Digital television, as opposed to traditional analogue services, expands the number of channels available by employing compression technology -- allowing a greater number of channels, for instance, to be bundled onto a single satellite transponder. The technology also provides better picture quality and CD-quality sound.

France led Western Europe in digital TV in 1996, although only one percent of French households claimed access to digital TV. Kagan World Media, however, forecasts that in 1997 France's digital penetration will climb to two percent, and Italy, Spain and Scandanavia will each post one percent penetration rates.
By the year 2000 Kagan expects digital TV to be in 10 percent of Western European television households, climbing to 32 percent in 2005.
As a result digital systems can offer up to 200 channels as opposed to the 20 or 30 channels offered by the average cable television company.
CORE PLAYERS IN EUROPE

Leading the charge for digital television in Western Europe are a core group of players, some of whom are using their existing businesses in analogue satellite services as building blocks for the digital world.
Some key companies are players in multiple television markets -- such as French pay-television company Canal Plus, satellite broadcaster British Sky Broadcasting, and Germany's Kirch Group.

Canal Plus, in addition to its French pay-TV service, is partnered with Bertelsmann and Kirch in Premiere, a German analogue satellite service that has plans for a digital pilot project. Canal Plus is also a partner in Spain's Canal Satellite Digital, which was launched in late January, along with Promotora de Informaciones (Prisa) and Antena 3.
In addition, Canal Plus in December agreed to merge with Dutch media group Nethold.

British Sky Broadcasting, controlled by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd and the UK's leading pay-TV provider with its analogue satellite service, has said it plans to buy up to a 49 percent stake in Germany's DF1, although BSkyB said earlier this month that some important issues had to be resolved.
BSkyB plans to launch its digital satellite service in Britain next autumn and is also a partner in a three-way joint venture that is bidding for one of Britain's digital terrestrial licences.

Both BSkyB and Canal Plus are using their digital ventures to accelerate a migration that is inevitable: both companies are running off of analogue satellites that will burn up in another three to four years.
NO ONE SET TO DOMINATE EUROPE'S DIGITAL LANDSCAPE
Despite the size of some of the players, no one has emerged to dominate the European digital landscape.

"It's going to be semi-fragmented," said Dennis Exton, a media analyst at Nikko Securities. "BSkyB will dominate in the UK...Canal Plus will dominate in France and in the Netherlands through Nethold. It will still possibly win in Germany, but will need Bertelsmann's help."
Premiere is battling against DFI, the fledgling satellite TV service controlled by Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch.

The Italian digital market remains up for grabs. Mediaset, the commercial television group controlled by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, and Telepiu, owned jointly by Nethold, Germany's Kirch as well as Berlusconi's Fininvest both are in position to be the ultimate winner, Exton said.

The fragmentation of the European market means the door remains open to non-European players -- most likely American companies such as DirecTV, the digital satellite broadcast service owned by Hughes Electronics Corp, and operator. Tele-Communications Inc, the largest U.S. cable TV operator.

DirecTV International, the sister company of DirecTV and its arm for development in all markets outside the U.S., signed a memorandum of understanding with the Spanish pay TV giant Sogecable last September to form a joint venture for digital TV in Spain. The memorandum expired without a definitive agreement reached.

"But we continue to pursue potential business partners in Europe," a spokeswoman for DirecTV International told Reuters. DirecTV International already has ventures in Latin America and is a partner in a venture to be launched in Japan later this year.
Jim Ramo, executive vice president for DirecTV, said he expects that any venture by the company in Europe would be done with a partner.

But while the early stages of digital television are dominated by arguments over whose set-top decoder box will control access to systems, industry observers and executives alike said that in the end programming content determines the battle for subscribers.
"If you can amass content you can attract the subscribers," said Chris Champion, a senior analyst with the Yankee Group.

"The driver in Europe is soccer and sports," said Kagan's Montgomery. "And a large part of the sustaining effort is movies...All the players are working very hard against each other to acquire the rights to the top Hollywood movies and the sports programming."
DirecTV's Ramo said the service's ability to offer 50 movies every night, with hit films showing every half hour, and its wide-ranging sports programming have been key contributors to its success.

DirecTV currently has about 2.3 million subscribers and expects to surpass its break-even point of three million subscribers later this year, a company spokesman said. Ramo said the average subscriber spends $40 a month, a figure which has been rising steadily.
Montgomery said DirecTV remains a likely player in Europe. "They have expertise in delivering programming," he said. "It would be a mistake to write them off."

With consumers facing ever-growing choices, so do advertisers. But while the market fragmentation may at first pose confusion, Nikko's Exton said he expects major, pan-European advertisers to use the growth in channels to bargain down ad rates.

"You'll get audience fragmentation," he said. "The advertising rates will get bargained down, meaning individual networks will have to consolidate down to maintain earnings. ...It's happening slowly already. But it's a long way from being a disaster level."
